crash_unjudged.label: Crash (not judged)
crash_unjudged.meaning: A check the reference never judged — the suite that measures what it needs was left out of the run, that measurement could not be made, or the reference cannot answer the check at all — that met this anyway. The check leaves the score as not applicable does, since the reference answered no such check, and the finding is counted and flags the row.
crash_unjudged.counted: counted as severe; excluded from the score

divergent.label: Different answer
divergent.meaning: Valid protocol, different answer from the reference: the silent kind a client may not notice

hang.label: Hang
hang.meaning: This session waited past the deadline; the server was otherwise alive

hang_unjudged.label: Hang (not judged)
hang_unjudged.meaning: A check the reference never judged — the suite that measures what it needs was left out of the run, that measurement could not be made, or the reference cannot answer the check at all — that met this anyway. The check leaves the score as not applicable does, since the reference answered no such check, and the finding is counted and flags the row.
hang_unjudged.counted: counted as severe; excluded from the score

harness_error.label: Not counted (our side)
harness_error.meaning: The measurement failed on our side, not the engine's. Also covers a missing answer that only our own probe saw after our client could not talk to the server at all. A bug of ours, fixed before publishing
harness_error.counted: excluded from the score; lowers coverage

not_applicable.label: Not applicable (counted elsewhere)
not_applicable.meaning: Left out of the score because something the check needs is missing and another check already counts that: a value type the engine refused, a TLS session, a pg_sleep that waits, the mechanism a per-type check repeats for one type (a binary cursor, a COPY format), or, in the access-method table, something the method did not provide (UPDATE, an index type). The gap is counted once, where it is measured; other checks do not count it again. A check that builds on the gap is still asked, and its answer carries this mark, so what the engine said is in the report while the gap stays counted once. Also a check that ran but could not be measured on this engine, with no gap shown (a query that completed before the CancelRequest meant for it reached the server), and the checks that needed it.
not_applicable.counted: excluded from the score and from coverage

observed.label: Unmeasured
observed.meaning: No reference recording for this check, so nothing to compare

protocol_violation.label: Protocol violation
protocol_violation.meaning: The server sent something the protocol forbids

skip.label: Skipped
skip.meaning: Not executed: a prerequisite this engine failed, a setup it rejected, or the target was down
skip.counted: denominator (counts against the score); lowers coverage

skip_excluded.label: Skipped (our side)
skip_excluded.meaning: Could not run because of something on our side, tracked as a bug of ours and fixed before publishing
skip_excluded.counted: excluded from the score; lowers coverage

unresponsive.label: Unresponsive
unresponsive.meaning: The port accepted TCP but the server stopped answering the protocol

unresponsive_unjudged.label: Unresponsive (not judged)
unresponsive_unjudged.meaning: A check the reference never judged — the suite that measures what it needs was left out of the run, that measurement could not be made, or the reference cannot answer the check at all — that met this anyway. The check leaves the score as not applicable does, since the reference answered no such check, and the finding is counted and flags the row.

unstable.label: Unstable
unstable.meaning: The check gave different outcomes in two identical runs: two campaigns on the same code, images and references. Neither outcome is the engine's answer, so the check is shown with both and left out of the score. A row with more than 10% of its judged checks unstable is not published.

unsupported.label: Refused

legend.scoring: Every check has one outcome. A role's score is the share of judgeable checks that matched the reference; failed prerequisites count as failures, because a client hits them too. Checks that failed on our side and checks with no reference recording are left out; a row where nothing is left has no score and says why in its note. The overall score weighs frames 0.315, types 0.135, bulk 0.225, upstream 0.135, catalog 0.1, conversions 0.09, renormalized over the roles that have a score; types and conversions share 0.225, all of it going to those of them that have a score when the others have none. Raw counts are published so any other weighting can be computed. role score = 100 × matched ÷ (checks − checks not counted against the engine − checks without a reference recording − checks needing a value type the engine lacks − unstable checks − crashes in checks the reference did not judge), with the counts summed over the role's suites, one decimal. overall = Σ weight × role score ÷ Σ weight over the roles that have a score (role scores rounded first), where roles that share a weight split it over those of them that have a score. coverage = 100 × (checks − skipped − not counted − needing a missing type − unstable − crashes not judged) ÷ (checks − needing a missing type − unstable − crashes not judged).
legend.baselines: Each engine is compared with a reference engine of the same protocol: the reference for the version it claims when one is recorded, otherwise the protocol default. The references in this dataset are, for elastic: elasticsearch-7, elasticsearch-8, elasticsearch-8-backpressure, elasticsearch-8-security, elasticsearch-9; for mongo: mongodb-6.0, mongodb-7.0, mongodb-8.0; for mysql: mysql-5.7, mysql-8.0, mysql-8.4, mysql-9; for pgwire: postgres-9.4, postgres-12, postgres-13, postgres-14, postgres-15, postgres-16, postgres-17, postgres-18; for redis: redis-6.2, redis-6.2-cluster, redis-6.2-node, redis-7.2, redis-7.2-cluster, redis-7.2-node, redis-8.2, redis-8.2-cluster, redis-8.2-node; for s3: ceph-rgw-21-dev. The row states which reference and why. Differences are counted as differences even when an engine documents them as intentional.
caveats: Tier 0 is the wire contract only: frames, types and bulk load. It is not the SQL dialect, performance, durability or feature coverage. A high score means drivers and tools can talk to the engine as they do to the reference; it does not mean your queries behave the same.

Checks talk to an engine the way the protocol's own clients do, SQL included: for PostgreSQL wire, the way PostgreSQL's test suites and pgx do, with :: casts, pg_sleep, generate_series and other PostgreSQL SQL. An engine that speaks the wire format with a different SQL dialect is measured as it answers that SQL; the finding names the construct. The Core column measures the same wire with standard SQL only, apart from these scores.
Scores are relative to a reference engine, not to a specification; a reference's own quirks are expected behavior here.
Results caused by our side never count against an engine. They are listed in each row's details, and a dataset that has any is not published.

A reference compared with its own recording should score 100; anything less is measurement noise we have to fix, and it bounds how precise the other rows are. References compared with another version show drift between versions of the same engine.
Each row is one run of one image (digest given) at one time. Other versions and configurations may differ.
The weights are a default, not a verdict. Every count is published so the scores can be recomputed.
Plain-words summaries are generated mechanically from the first difference of each root cause; the check ids and the observed-vs-expected example are the evidence.
Reproduce a row: stroppy-conformity run -t <target> --protocol <protocol> --baseline <reference>, or one check with --check <check id>, using the tool version and image digest the details give.

Contest a finding by opening an issue at github.com/stroppy-io/stroppy-conformity with the check id and run id. Findings are evidence, not opinion: the run id names the full report, frame traces included, and a confirmed bug on our side is fixed and the row re-measured.

The access-method table compares a table access method with heap in the same server image and version, so changes the image makes to the server itself are not counted against the method. Rows of a statement without ORDER BY compare as a multiset there, since a method may return them in its own order. Its overall score weighs upstream 0.15, access_method 0.85.

A variant row (variant set) runs an engine with a switch its vendor documents for compatibility, against the same reference as the engine as shipped. It is a row of its own and never part of the engine's own score. Its column vs. as shipped is its overall score minus that of the engine as shipped on the same protocol, in points. When the engine does not take the switch, that one check counts and every other check of the variant is not applicable.

The forks table lists engines built from another engine's source beside that upstream engine's reference of the same major version, as the version the fork reports names it. A fork's differences from upstream can be intentional; they are still listed as differences. A fork that numbers its releases on its own has no upstream release of the same major and is read against the reference its row was compared with, which the table says. The backup tools in the table are server-internal ones, run on the fork's server and on the upstream reference beside it: the upstream engine's own where upstream ships one, and the fork vendor's where the vendor backs its server up with its own instead (Percona XtraBackup, Percona Backup for MongoDB), so a row whose two sides run the same tool compares the tool no less than the engine. A step that completes on the reference and not on the fork is a finding, listed in the table and part of no score.

The engine-family table reads the engines built from one source line against each other: every member of a family is compared check by check with the family's baseline target, and the two rows' outcomes are read side by side. It is a second comparison of its own: a member's default scores are the ones its row was measured for, and the table changes none of them. Only checks both rows ran from the same upstream test files, with both answers judged against their references, are compared; a check one row ran and the other did not, a check one of the two answers was not judged on (a skip, a result void on our side, no reference recording, an outcome that changed between two identical runs, what a target's plan gave up) and a check the two rows ran from different upstream test files are counted apart. A difference here is a difference between two engines of one family, and it can be intentional.

Same answers are counted on the checks both rows judged. Each row is graded against its own reference, so an upstream change both engines carry shows as the same answer. These checks use PostgreSQL SQL and the PostgreSQL protocol, so the share is PostgreSQL-level. Greenplum-specific SQL (DISTRIBUTED BY, append-optimized tables, partitions, the gp_* catalogs, external tables, resource management, gp_toolkit) is measured by pgwire.greenplum, which is informational and in no score yet.

A row whose two rows were graded against different references shows no share: 'both matched their own reference' would then read as the two engines answering alike, which it does not mean. The suites where their answers part are listed instead.

legend.feature_cells: feature_cells[k] describes features[feature_sets[protocol][k]] for a row of that protocol: null when the row has no check of that feature, otherwise [code, matched, total]. code is the worst outcome (legend.feature_codes; higher is worse), matched the checks that matched, total the checks that count toward a score (the role score's denominator); a total of 0 is the not-applicable code when every check was left out by design, the unmeasured one otherwise.
legend.supported_types_filter: Filter out unsupported types: re-scores every row without the checks that need a value type the engine does not support, meaning its type check was refused, or could not run because a type it needs is missing. A type the engine supports but encodes differently from the reference is kept, and its differences still count. Off by default; the numbers it shows are published beside the default ones as scores_supported_types and counts_supported_types.
legend.core_profile: Core: the same wire contract measured with standard SQL only. It counts the checks that send no SQL (startup, authentication, raw frames) or only standard SQL, and the standard-SQL copies of checks whose SQL is the protocol's own dialect (a :: cast, pg_sleep, generate_series), recorded from the same reference. Scores, coverage and weights follow the default rules over those checks. The default scores never include the copies and do not change with Core. Shown only for protocols whose checks say which SQL they send (PostgreSQL wire); published as scores_core and counts_core. The unsupported-types filter does not change it: Core checks need no type that only a dialect check establishes.
